newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia diesel at 4-mth low, early recovery unlikely.
newsitem.headline: Asia diesel at 4-mth low, early recovery unlikely.

text.p: Asian diesel prices have fallen below $30.00 per barrel for the first time in four months and are unlikely to recover soon, industry sources said on Wednesday.
"The market lost $3-$4 per barrel in a week because China stopped buying and the weather. I am not sure if we have seen the bottom," a trader at a major oil refiner said.
Traders said the market was likely to hover below the $30.00 mark at least until after the Chinese New Year holidays at the beginning of February before showing some recovery in March.

Diesel proces have fallen sharply, from near six-year highs of $34.45 per barrel in early December to $30.65 last Friday. Sellers have since offered diesel as low as $29.00, the first time it has been below $30 since October 24, but buyers are holding back.
"We are trying to find where the market is. Demand has disappeared," another refining source said.
Traders said the fall was prompted by a combination of bearish factors.
Asian refining capacity rose about one million barrels per day in 1996 to 17.5 million bpd -- which means more oil products are up for sale.
Western prices for heating oil and gas oil fell sharply when the U.S. and Europe started to thaw out from unseasonally cold weather.

And China, which had absorbed higher South Korean exports, cut back on its buying. In December and January, China imported an estimated one million tonnes per month to cover a shortage, triple its average of about 370,000 tonnes per month.
"China had been supporting the market for the past four months but they are just not buying. They are all covered until after the (Chinese) New Year," one source said.
Traders said the loss of China's support has led to some panic selling. "The market is very shaky right now as China is not buying," said one.
China's absence comes at a time when diesel production is at a seasonal peak because of high demand for heating.
In addition, South Korea has beefed up its refinery capacity. The country added 450,000 barrels per day in December alone.
South Korea's December and January spot exports amounted to between 250,000-300,000 tonnes, about 30 percent more than its normal monthly exports.
Traders said the extra production from South Korea was now a cause for concern in the absence of China's buying.
Refiners in Singapore, Thailand and Taiwan are looking for sales outlets of their late January and February cargoes of diesel, adding to the near-term bearish sentiment.
Traders said the market might not pick up until the end of the first quarter, when the closure of two Singapore refineries for maintenance is expected to tighten supply.
Mobil is due to shut down its 280,000 barrel per day (bpd) refinery in March, while Singapore Refining Co will shut down a 90,000 bpd crude unit for three weeks beginning March 1.
